Good morning, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician whose whole job is to support moms in the weeks and months after birth. Today I’d like to do a gentle check-in using a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days, so we can be sure you’re getting any support you might need. Everything you share stays confidential between you and the care team, and we’ll take it at your pace in a safe, judgment-free space. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past seven days: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has laughter felt hard to come by?

Um… I guess I’ve still been able to laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Like, if my husband makes a silly joke I’ll smile, but it feels kind of muted—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of it just happening naturally.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes... but it's not the same easy laugh I used to have. I might chuckle if something's really funny, yet it feels kind of forced—like I'm working to find the humor instead of just feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings dinner—but the excitement isn’t as strong as before. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” rather than really counting down the hours.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong or that a “better mom” would know how to fix it. It’s not every minute, but those thoughts pop in more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly feel a wave of worry—like I need to check the baby’s breathing even though he’s fine—but I can usually talk myself down after a minute or two. It’s not constant, but it shows up out of nowhere a couple of times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky… more like a quick rush of “what if something bad happens?” It passes pretty fast once I take a deep breath or remind myself we’re both okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes. I’ll be trying to fold laundry while the baby stirs in the bassinet, and suddenly it feels like the pile is huge and I’ll never get through the day. It usually eases once I tick one small task off the list, but yeah—there are moments when everything feels heavier than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I haven’t felt that unhappy. I do have nights where it takes me a while to fall asleep—my mind keeps running through the next day’s feedings and chores—but it’s not because I’m overwhelmingly sad or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’ve had a few stretches, mostly in the evenings, where I just feel kind of down and weepy. It’s not all day, but yesterday I cried for a bit when my partner asked how I was doing—said I was “fine,” but inside I just felt blah and heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

That’s happened a couple of times this week. Nothing huge set me off—once it was just seeing a messy kitchen and feeling like I couldn’t keep up. I cried for a few minutes, felt a little better after, but yeah, the tears have come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that has crossed my mind. I’ve felt tired or overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Patient responses reveal:
- Reduced ability to experience pleasure/enjoyment (laughing, looking forward to activities)
- Episodic low mood with tearfulness, especially evenings
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care
- Intermittent, situational anxiety/worry without clear trigger; no frank panic attacks
- Moments of feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; resolves with small accomplishments
- Mild sleep-onset delay related to “mental to-do list,” not attributed to sadness
- No self-harm ideation

Overall pattern: sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms of mild intensity, present several days per week, without functional incapacity or safety concerns. Consider formal PHQ-9/EPDS and continued monitoring for possible postpartum depression and/or anxiety.
